title: Classifying living things
summary: How are living things grouped, and how are species named?
cards.0.p: More than one and a half million species of living things have been named so far. Classification means grouping living things by shared traits. This makes it easier to identify them, see how they are related and share information.
cards.0.key: Classification means grouping living things by shared traits.
cards.0.once.soru: About how many species of living things have been named on Earth?
cards.0.once.secenekler.0.neden: New species are found every year too. Memorizing so many species one by one is impossible. That is why we group living things.
cards.0.once.secenekler.1.neden: There are more than 10000 bird species alone.
cards.0.once.secenekler.2.neden: The number of insect species alone is close to a million.
cards.1.p: Artificial classification looks at appearance. So it puts the bat and the eagle in a "flyers" group. Natural classification looks at relatedness and compares homologous organs, embryos and DNA. By this classification, the bat is a mammal.
cards.1.key: Homologous organs have the same origin (a human arm and a bat wing). Analogous organs only have the same job (a bird wing and an insect wing).
cards.1.once.soru: Both bats and eagles fly. But a bat gives birth to live young and feeds them milk. Which group does the bat belong to?
cards.1.once.secenekler.0.neden: By natural classification, which looks at relatedness, the bat is a mammal. Its wing has the same origin as a human arm.
cards.1.once.secenekler.1.neden: Flying is a shared job, but it does not show relatedness. Bats have no feathers and nurse their young.
cards.1.once.secenekler.2.neden: A bat has a skeleton and is not closely related to insects.
cards.2.p: Living things are placed in nested levels. From broadest to narrowest, these levels are: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. The basic unit of classification is the species.
cards.2.svg#0: Where humans fit: from most general to most specific
cards.2.key: Domain > kingdom > phylum > class > order > family > genus > species
cards.2.etk.soru: Starting from kingdom, order the levels from broadest to narrowest.
cards.3.p: Moving down toward species, the number of species in a group decreases, while shared traits and relatedness increase. Living things that share a level also share every level above it. The reverse is not always true.
cards.3.svg#11: Moving up toward kingdom reverses them all
cards.3.key: As the level narrows, it is the number of species that decreases, not the number of individuals.
cards.4.h: What is a species? The mule example
cards.4.p: In sexually reproducing organisms, a species is made up of individuals that can mate with each other and produce fertile offspring. The fact that mules are sterile shows that horses and donkeys are separate species. In bacteria, species are told apart by their DNA.
cards.4.svg#8: same species: offspring can reproduce too
cards.4.svg#16: different species: offspring is born but can't reproduce
cards.4.svg#17: Horses and donkeys are separate species
cards.4.key: If the offspring is not fertile, its parents are not of the same species.
cards.5.p: Linnaeus gave each species a two-word Latin name. First comes the genus name with a capital letter, then the species name in lowercase. The name is written in italics: Homo sapiens.
cards.5.svg#0: Scientific name = two words, Latin, italic
cards.5.key: The genus name starts with a capital letter and the species name with a lowercase letter, and both are written in italics: Panthera leo.
cards.6.p: Living things are first divided into three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryotes. The first two are prokaryotes. But archaea are not bacteria and are more closely related to eukaryotes.
cards.6.key: There are six kingdoms: Bacteria, Archaea, Protists, Plants, Fungi and Animals.
cards.6.once.soru: Bacteria and archaea are both single-celled organisms with no nucleus. Are they in the same group?
cards.6.once.secenekler.0.neden: Their cell walls and some of their molecules differ. By DNA, archaea are closer to eukaryotes than bacteria are.
cards.6.once.secenekler.1.neden: Having no nucleus is a shared trait, but archaea are not bacteria.
cards.6.once.secenekler.2.neden: Archaea are cellular organisms, not viruses.
cards.7.p: Bacteria and archaea are both single-celled prokaryotes. Bacteria have peptidoglycan in their cell walls, and archaea do not. Bacteria break down wastes, fix nitrogen and can cause disease. Archaea often live in extremely hot or salty places.
cards.7.key: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on viruses.
cards.8.p: Eukaryotes that are not plants, fungi or animals are called protists. Plants have cellulose walls and carry out photosynthesis. Fungi have chitin walls. They digest food outside themselves and absorb it. Animals have no cell wall.
cards.8.key: The cell wall is made of cellulose in plants and chitin in fungi. Animal cells have no wall.
cards.9.p: Most protists are single-celled. The amoeba moves with false feet, and the paramecium moves with cilia. Euglena carries out photosynthesis in light and takes in ready-made food in the dark. Plasmodium causes malaria.
cards.9.svg#9: Plasmodium: causes malaria · Algae: producers in water
cards.9.key: Euglena can feed both as an autotroph and as a heterotroph.
cards.9.once.soru: Euglena carries out photosynthesis in light and takes in ready-made food in the dark. Which kingdom is it in?
cards.9.once.secenekler.0.neden: Euglena is a single-celled eukaryote. It does not belong to the plant or animal kingdom.
cards.9.once.secenekler.1.neden: Euglena carries out photosynthesis, but it is single-celled and also takes in ready-made food. So it is not a plant.
cards.9.once.secenekler.2.neden: Euglena takes in ready-made food, but it has chloroplasts. So it is not an animal.
cards.10.p: Most fungi are multicellular and made of threads called hyphae. Most break down dead remains. Yeast makes bread rise. A lichen is a fungus and an alga living together. The alga makes food, and the fungus protects the alga.
cards.10.key: A lichen is not a kingdom but a partnership between a fungus and an alga. Lichens are very sensitive to air pollution.
cards.10.once.soru: Lichens that live on bare rock are actually a partnership of two organisms. Which two?
cards.10.once.secenekler.0.neden: The alga makes food by photosynthesis. The fungus holds water and protects the alga.
cards.10.once.secenekler.1.neden: A lichen is neither a plant nor an animal.
cards.10.once.secenekler.2.neden: One partner can be a cyanobacterium, but the other is always a fungus.
cards.11.h: Why aren't viruses in any kingdom?
cards.11.p: As you saw in the first topic, viruses are not cells. Kingdoms were set up for cellular organisms. So viruses are not placed in any kingdom and are studied separately.
cards.11.key: A virus can multiply only inside a host cell.
cards.11.once.soru: Why aren't viruses placed in any kingdom?
cards.11.once.secenekler.0.neden: Kingdoms were set up for cellular organisms. A virus is not a cell, so it is studied separately.
cards.11.once.secenekler.1.neden: Bacteria are small too, but they belong to a kingdom. The test is being a cell, not size.
cards.11.once.secenekler.2.neden: Being harmful is not a classification criterion.
cards.12.p:
• Science uses natural classification, based on relatedness.
• Moving down toward species, the number of species decreases, and shared traits and relatedness increase.
• Individuals that can produce fertile offspring belong to the same species. The mule is sterile.
• The binomial name is written in italics, and the genus starts with a capital letter.
• There are three domains and six kingdoms. Viruses are not in any kingdom.
cards.12.svg#11: kingdom › phylum › class › order › family › genus › species
cards.12.svg#12: Toward species: more shared traits, fewer species
quiz.0.q: Find where humans fit in classification. Match each level with the human group at that level.
quiz.0.e: Humans are in the animal kingdom, the chordate phylum, the mammal class, the primate order and the genus Homo. The species name is Homo sapiens.
quiz.1.q: Put each organism in its kingdom.
quiz.1.e: A cyanobacterium is a bacterium that carries out photosynthesis. The amoeba, euglena, paramecium and plasmodium are single-celled eukaryotic protists. Yeast, mold and mushrooms are in the fungus kingdom.
quiz.2.q: Match each term with its correct description.
quiz.2.ciftler.0.1: Those that can produce fertile offspring
quiz.2.ciftler.1.1: First word of a binomial name
quiz.2.e: Individuals that can produce fertile offspring form a species, and the first word of a binomial name is the genus. Natural classification looks at relatedness, and artificial classification at appearance. The broadest level is the domain.
quiz.3.q: Which is an example of homologous organs?
quiz.3.o.0: A bird wing and a fly wing
quiz.3.o.1: A human arm and a whale flipper
quiz.3.o.2: A bat wing and a butterfly wing
quiz.3.o.3: A rose thorn and a hedgehog spine
quiz.3.e: A human arm and a whale flipper come from the same bone layout. Their origin is the same, but their jobs differ. Natural classification looks at similarities like this.
quiz.3.y.0: Both are for flying, but their origins differ. These are analogous organs.
quiz.3.y.2: Their jobs are the same, but their origins differ. This is a pair of analogous organs.
quiz.3.y.3: The plant's thorn and the animal's spine are only similar in job. Their origins are completely different.
A:ozet: Try first, then learn the name. Move down the levels, watch the mule, fix a name and identify an organism with a key.
A:adimlar.0.metin: Living things are sorted into nested groups, and one of the narrowest is the genus. Move down the levels toward the house cat. Stop when you find the organism in the same genus as the house cat.
A:adimlar.0.gorev.tamam: This genus is called Felis, and it includes the house cat and the wildcat. Even the lion was left out of this genus.
A:adimlar.1.baslik: Same family, not the same genus
A:adimlar.1.metin: The lion and the house cat are in the same family: both are felids. Move up and down the levels and see which groups they share.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.soru: Which is certainly true for two organisms in the same family?
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.yazi: They are in the same genus
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Below family is the genus level. The lion is in the genus Panthera, and the house cat in Felis.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: They are in the same order
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Organisms that share a level also share every level above it: order, class, phylum and kingdom. The reverse is not true.
A:adimlar.1.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: The fertile offspring test defines a species. The lion and the house cat are in the same family but are different species.
A:adimlar.2.metin: When a female horse and a male donkey mate, a mule is born. Predict before you press play.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.soru: Can mules mate with each other and have offspring?
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: A mule is not a new species. It is a sterile hybrid of a horse and a donkey.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.yazi: Only if it mates with a horse
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: The problem is not the mate but the mule itself. A mule cannot make proper sex cells.
A:adimlar.2.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: A horse has 64 chromosomes and a donkey 62. A mule has 63, so it cannot make proper sex cells.
A:adimlar.3.metin: Every species has a two-word Latin name: the genus first, then the species name. The genus starts with a capital letter, the species name with a lowercase letter, and the name is in italics. Now fix the wolf's name.
A:adimlar.3.gorev.tamam: The correct form is Canis lupus. First comes the genus (Canis), then the species name that identifies the species (lupus). The dog is in the same genus as the wolf. When writing by hand, each of the two words is underlined separately instead of using italics.
A:adimlar.4.metin: You can find an organism's kingdom with questions about its cell structure. Bread mold has a nucleus, and its cell wall contains chitin.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.soru: Which kingdom is bread mold in?
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Plant cell walls are made of cellulose, and plants carry out photosynthesis. Mold does not carry out photosynthesis.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: An organism with a nucleus and a chitin wall is a fungus. Mold, yeast and mushrooms are in the same kingdom.
A:adimlar.4.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: Bacteria have no nucleus. Mold cells do have a nucleus.
A:adimlar.5.metin: A single-celled organism was found in a hot spring. Its cell has no nucleus, and its cell wall has no peptidoglycan. Use the key to find its group.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.soru: Which group is this organism in?
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.0.neden: Bacteria have peptidoglycan in their cell walls. This organism's wall does not.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.1.neden: Fungi are eukaryotes, and their cells have a nucleus.
A:adimlar.5.gorev.secenekler.2.neden: An organism with no nucleus and no peptidoglycan in its wall is an archaeon. A hot spring is also one of the extreme places where archaea live.
A:kapanis.0: Science uses natural classification, based on relatedness, that is, common ancestry.
A:kapanis.1: From broadest to narrowest, the levels are domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species. Moving down toward species, the number of species decreases, and shared traits and relatedness increase.
A:kapanis.2: Individuals that can produce fertile offspring with each other belong to the same species. Because the mule is sterile, horses and donkeys are separate species.
A:kapanis.3: The binomial name is written in italics. The genus name starts with a capital letter and the species name with a lowercase letter: Homo sapiens.
A:kapanis.4: There are three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryotes. Viruses are not cells, so they belong to no kingdom.
